content: QR-as-anchor has a well-characterised threat model. Sartayeva et al. name three attacks: (a) QR code replacement - an adversary swaps the physical code for one containing malicious content or an incorrect location, hard to detect unless landmarks are monitored, so the literature recommends letting users report corruption through the localisation app and physically shielding codes; (b) replay / location faking - the user photographs the code or generates their own with the same data, so the fix is a validity period inside the code (minutes) or verifying against GPS; (c) physical QR corruption, which is easy to detect and should be user-reportable. Cryptographic mitigations from production systems: QRAuth signs payloads with HMAC-SHA256 truncated to 16 hex characters (64 bits) for animated codes and explicitly caps the length because 'a longer token would stretch the QR URL onto a denser module grid, shrinking each printed square below what a phone reads reliably at arm's length' - direct precedent for the project's hmac8 design and for not lengthening the payload; it also implements replay prevention by rejecting previously seen frame indices and a +/-5 second freshness window. PreArrive uses the same pattern: HMAC-SHA256 truncated to 64 bits over reservation_id|signed_at|content_hash, with the server secret never leaving the server, and notes that 64 bits of HMAC is far beyond what is needed against a rate-limited online verification endpoint. Also relevant: QRAuth's protocol-design page states plainly that client-reported geolocation is 'a client-reported signal, not a cryptographic guarantee' - i.e. no amount of QR signing makes the scan itself proof of physical presence, so the honest security claim for this project is 'the code cannot be forged to point at a node that does not exist', not 'the system proves where the user is'. Fingerprinting the payload and looking it up server-side (rather than trusting a client-supplied node id) is the mechanism that lets codes be retired server-side without reprinting.
